title: Nature of Party System in India
shortDescription: Features of the multi-party system, recognition criteria, Tenth Schedule and party finance.
genZNote: One party ruled for decades, then coalitions, then dominance again — India's party system is multi-party with plot twists. Know the criteria and the anti-defection law.

sections.heading: Nature of the Party System
bullets: India has a multi-party system with national and state parties; the "Congress system" (dominant-party phase until 1967), coalition era after 1989, and later dominance of a party/alliance in elections.
Functions: aggregating interests, forming governments, opposition, mobilisation, policy formulation.
Registration of parties under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951; recognition and symbols under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.

sections.heading: Recognition and Anti-Defection
bullets: National party (ECI criteria): recognised as a state party in four or more states; or 6% valid votes in four or more states in a Lok Sabha/assembly election plus 4 Lok Sabha seats; or 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11) from at least three states. State party criteria are lower.

Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985): disqualification for defection; 91st Amendment (2003) removed the "one-third split" exemption — a merger needs two-thirds of the legislature party; presiding officer decides (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992: subject to judicial review).
Party finance: donations through electoral bonds were struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024; transparency and disclosure remain key issues.
National party list changes after elections — check the latest ECI notification.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.body: Dynastic politics, money power, criminalisation, lack of internal democracy, personality-centred parties and defections; responses include ECI directions, disclosure of criminal antecedents and electoral reforms.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: India has a competitive multi-party system regulated by ECI recognition rules and the Tenth Schedule against defection.

highYieldFacts: Merger needs two-thirds of legislature party.
commonTraps: Do not say the Tenth Schedule bars all floor-crossing without exceptions.
